newsitem.title: IRAQ: More food under oil deal arrives in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: More food under oil deal arrives in Iraq.

text.p: Iraq has received over 600,000 tonnes of food since its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations went into effect in December, a U.N. official said on Tuesday.

The official said a total of 20 ships carrying foodstuffs under Iraq's oil-for-food deal have anchored at the port of Umm Qasr since December. Supplies were also reaching Iraq via border posts with both Turkey and Jordan, he said.
He said the U.N. sanctions committee has so far approved more than 160 contracts for supplying Iraq with food and medicine under the deal.
"Two ships arrived recently. One yesterday carrying 22,500 tonnes of Thai rice and another on May 11 carrying 13,500 tonnes of Australian wheat," the official said.
"In total 660,000 tonnes of supplies have reached the country, 490,000 of the them via Iraq's main port of Umm Qasr."
"Momentum continues to build up," said the U.N. official, adding that two ships with French sugar were scheduled to arrive late in May.

Iraqis have not yet received a full basket of rations under the deal, which allows Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy urgent needs for Iraqis, suffering from U.N. sanctions imposed for Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Sugar rations have not yet been distributed but the official said 50,000 tonnes of sugar were expected to be in Iraq by the end of June.

Iraq's plan was to import 255,564 tonnes of sugar to meet needs for six months. It has allocated $115 million from its oil money to sugar imports to cover the new sugar ration of 2 kg. (4.4 lb) per person.
Iraq has received the first shipment of medical supplies last week.

Iraq has earmarked $210 million for medical supplies and another 10 million for health repairs. Iraqi officials have been complaining about delays in the arrival of humanitarian goods particularly medical supplies.

It has also allocated more than $870 million of the $1.3 billion of the money left for it under the oil sales for food imports. It needs to pay 30 per cent to a U.N. reparations fund and meet other U.N. costs.
Iraqi newspapers published a report on Tuesday saying President Saddam Hussein and his cabinet discussed the obstacles the United States was putting on the way to implementing the deal.
In May Iraqis received additional rations of wheat, flour, rice, legumes, baby milk, cooking oil, soap and detergent powder. They still have not received a full ration of tea and sugar.
The oil deal which went into effect in December will come for review in June and Iraq had hoped to be able to buy the 2.2 million tonnes of humanitarian supplies it contracted for.
